intent: Show that two people can have the same job and similar income, yet one has far more accumulated wealth, making equal income taxation an incomplete picture.

requirements.question: How do the two labeled bars compare accumulated wealth?
Why is equal income taxation insufficient despite the wealth gap?

units.claim: MY WEALTH is much smaller than FRIEND'S WEALTH; the friend's labeled bar is more than four times as tall.
accept: both MY WEALTH and FRIEND'S WEALTH are shown as labeled bars
FRIEND'S WEALTH is clearly and substantially taller than MY WEALTH
the visual gap is roughly four times or more
reject: omitting either bar or either label
showing the two wealth levels as equal
units.evidence: Two axis-free labeled bars: MY WEALTH is about 104 px tall and FRIEND'S WEALTH about 442 px tall in the clean source frame.

units.hardcase_reason: The chart directly visualizes only the wealth gap; the similar job, income, and income-tax treatment are supplied by the narration.
units.claim: The two people have similar income and therefore similar income-tax burdens, even though their accumulated wealth differs sharply.
accept: the two people have the same job and about the same income
their income is taxed about the same
their accumulated wealth remains sharply unequal despite the similar income tax
reject: saying the friend pays much more income tax solely because of greater accumulated wealth
saying the two people have equal wealth
omitting the wealth gap when making the income-tax point
units.evidence: Narration-only context. Do not invent a visual income bar or a tax-rate mark that is absent from the source chart.

g0_data_completeness.selection: all role=bar data rows; annotation rows excluded

clip_hardcase.reason: The equal-income premise cannot be derived from the two wealth bars alone.

hardcases.handling: must_be_visualized=false; preserve the claim through narration and do not invent an income bar or tax mark.
